quickRef.title: Right-triangle height
quickRef.intro: Take a right triangle and drop a line from the right-angle corner $C$ **straight down** to the long side $AB$ (the hypotenuse). That line is the height $h$. It cuts the long side into two pieces, $p$ and $q$, so the whole long side is $c=p+q$. It also splits the triangle into two smaller triangles with the **same shape** as the big one, which is why these four shortcuts work. Check them on a 3-4-5 triangle: $p=1.8$, $q=3.2$, $h=2.4$.

formats.title: Quantitative Comparison
rules: Your job is to try to **break** it. Try two very different numbers. If the winner changes, the answer is (D).
Good numbers to try: $0$, $1$, $-1$, $\frac12$, a big number, and both ends of any allowed range.
No letters, just numbers? Then it can't be (D). Just work it out.
Picture 'not drawn to scale' shapes stretched or squished in every way the facts allow.

formats.title: Multiple choice, one answer
rules: Look at the answers first. They tell you how exact you need to be.
Stuck setting it up? Try the middle answer in the question and see if it's too big or too small.
No numbers given? Make some up (like 100 for percents).
The wrong answers are built from common mistakes, so finding your number among the choices doesn't prove it's right.

formats.title: Select all that apply
rules: All or nothing: no partial credit. Judge each choice yes/no on its own.
First find the rule (a range, 'multiples of 47', 'odd numbers from 5 to 65'), then test every choice against it, including **both ends**.
Picking every choice is almost never right. Look for the one built to fail.

formats.title: Numeric Entry
rules: There are no choices to catch a mistake, so reread the last sentence and **underline what they're asking for**.
Plug your answer back into the question to check it.
Fractions don't need simplifying. Negative answers are allowed.

formats.title: Charts & tables
rules: Read the title, labels and units before you start.
Estimate first. The answers are often far apart.
For 'percent of' and 'percent more than', check what you're dividing by.

pacing: About **1:45 per question**: 12 questions in 21 minutes, then 15 in 26.
If you're at **2:30** with no plan, guess, mark it, and move on. You can come back.
Do the easy ones first; come back to marked ones with the time you saved.
Practice with the timer on (exam mode), so your score is real.
A 170 means 0–2 mistakes. The easiest points to win back are comparison traps and misreading the question.

sections.title: Circles & shapes inside circles
sections.idea: Almost every circle problem is a **right triangle** in disguise. Draw a line from the center to a point on the circle: that's the radius, and it's usually the long side of a right triangle.

example.q: A square has all four corners on a circle of radius 5. What is the area of the square?
steps: The square's diagonal (corner to corner) goes straight across the circle, so the diagonal is $2\times5=10$.
A square with diagonal $d$ has area $\frac{d^2}{2}$.
Area $=\frac{100}{2}=50$. (Quick check with the shortcut: $2r^2=2\times25=50$.)

facts: **Square inside a circle:** the diagonal = the circle's width ($2r$). Area $=2r^2$.
**Circle inside a square:** the circle touches all four sides, so the side $=2r$. Area $=4r^2$.
Square in a circle in a square: each square is exactly **half** the one around it.
**Square in a half-circle** (standing on the flat edge): area $=\frac45r^2$. Why: a top corner is $\frac s2$ across and $s$ up from the center, so $\left(\frac s2\right)^2+s^2=r^2$.
**Chord** = a straight line across the circle. A line from the center that meets it at a right angle cuts it exactly **in half**.
**Arc** = part of the edge. Arc $=\frac{\text{center angle}}{360}\times2\pi r$.
A line that just touches the circle (a tangent) makes a right angle with the radius.

**Circle inside a triangle** (touches all three sides): $r=\frac{\text{Area}}{s}$, where $s$ is half the perimeter. Right triangle: $r=\frac{a+b-c}{2}$. Equilateral with side $a$: $r=\frac{\sqrt3}{6}a$.

**Triangle inside a circle** (all three corners on it): $R=\frac{abc}{4\times\text{Area}}$. Right triangle: $R=\frac c2$, half the hypotenuse. Equilateral: $R=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}a$, exactly **twice** $r$.

**Excircle** (outside the triangle, touching one side and the other two sides extended): $r_a=\frac{\text{Area}}{s-a}$. Right triangle: the one beyond the hypotenuse has radius $s$; the one beyond leg $a$ has $s-b$. Equilateral: $r_a=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}a$, the height itself.
tricks: Stuck? Draw the radius to every point that's on the circle and look for the right triangle.
Two chords on **opposite sides** of the center: the gap between them is their two distances from the center **added together**.
If half the chord is $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ times the radius, you have a 30-60-90 triangle. The angle at the center in that triangle is $60^\circ$, so the full center angle is $120^\circ$.
Equilateral triangle: inside radius, outside radius and height are $1:2:3$. The center sits one third of the way up the height.
traps: Using the diameter as the square's **side**. It's the square's **diagonal** that equals the diameter.
Using the angle from your right triangle (half the center angle) as the full center angle. Double it first, or your arc comes out half as long.
Using the whole chord in the triangle. Always use **half** the chord.
Using the whole perimeter in $r=\frac{\text{Area}}{s}$. The $s$ is **half** the perimeter.

tips.title: A diameter side means a right angle
tips.text: **When:** a triangle has all three corners on a circle, and one of its sides goes straight through the center (a diameter). **Then:** the corner across from that side is $90^\circ$. The diameter is the longest side of a right triangle, so Pythagoras works.
tips.example: $AB$ is a diameter of length $10$, $AC=6$, and $C$ is on the circle. Angle $C=90^\circ$, so $BC=\sqrt{10^2-6^2}=\sqrt{64}=8$.

tips.text: **When:** an angle has its corner on the circle itself, not at the center. **Then:** it is **half** the center angle that opens onto the same arc. Move the corner anywhere else on the far side of the circle and the angle doesn't change.
tips.example: The center angle is $120^\circ$. Every angle with its corner on the circle that opens onto the same arc is $\frac{120}{2}=60^\circ$.

tips.title: Circle inside vs. circle around a triangle
tips.text: **Circle inside** (it touches all three sides): $r=\frac{\text{Area}}{s}$, with $s$ = half the perimeter. **Circle around** (all three corners on it): $R=\frac{abc}{4\times\text{Area}}$. **Right triangle:** $r=\frac{a+b-c}{2}$ and $R=\frac c2$. **Equilateral, side $a$:** $r=\frac{\sqrt3}{6}a$ and $R=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}a=2r$.
tips.example: Sides $3,4,5$: Area $=6$, $s=6$. So $r=\frac66=1$ (check: $\frac{3+4-5}{2}=1$) and $R=\frac{3\cdot4\cdot5}{4\cdot6}=2.5$ (check: $\frac52$).

tips.text: **When:** a circle sits outside the triangle, touching one side and the **other two sides extended**. **Then:** $r_a=\frac{\text{Area}}{s-a}$, where $a$ is the side it touches. **Right triangle:** beyond the hypotenuse the radius is $s$ itself; beyond leg $a$ it is $s-b$. **Equilateral:** $r_a=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}a$, the height, so 3 times the inside radius.

sections.title: Triangles
sections.idea: Learn two special triangles by heart. Most hard triangle questions are one of them in disguise; you just have to **cut the shape** the right way.

example.q: In triangle $ABC$, angle $B=30^\circ$ and side $BC=8$. How long is the height from $C$ straight down to side $AB$?
steps: Drop the height from $C$. On the $B$ side you get a 30-60-90 triangle, and $BC=8$ is its longest side.
In a 30-60-90 triangle, the side across from $30^\circ$ is **half** the longest side.
The height is across from the $30^\circ$ angle, so it is $\frac82=4$.

facts: **45-45-90** (half a square): sides $1:1:\sqrt2$. The long side = short side $\times\sqrt2$.
**30-60-90** (half an equilateral triangle): sides $1:\sqrt3:2$. The shortest side is across from $30^\circ$, and the longest is twice that.
**Area** $=\frac12\times$ base $\times$ height, and **any** side can be the base. So the height to a side $=\frac{2\times\text{area}}{\text{that side}}$.
Any two sides add up to **more** than the third side.

**Longest side theorem** (angle-side rule): the **biggest angle** is across from the **longest side**, and the **smallest angle** is across from the **shortest side**. It works both ways, and equal sides face equal angles.
Whole-number right triangles to know: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, and their multiples like 6-8-10.
tricks: Not a right triangle? **Drop a height** to split it into two special right triangles.
'Not drawn to scale' means don't trust your eyes. Imagine stretching the shape every way the facts still allow.
traps: Assuming an angle is $90^\circ$ just because it looks like one.
Assuming a line hits the middle, or is a height, when the question never says so.
Forgetting the $\frac12$ in the area.
Treating the angle-side rule as a ratio. It only puts sides and angles in the **same order**: twice the angle does not mean twice the side.

Overhanging triangle (an angle over $90^\circ$ at the base): using the slanted side as the height, or adding the overhang to the base. The height drops onto the **extended** base line; the base stays the original side.

tips.title: Slide the top corner: the area stays the same
tips.text: **When:** triangles share a base, and their top corners all sit on a line **parallel** to that base. **Then:** they all have the same height, so the same area. Slide the top corner along the line until you get a right triangle, which is easier to work with.
tips.example: Base $8$, top corner on a line $5$ above the base. Area $=\frac12\times8\times5=20$, however slanted the triangle is.

tips.title: Two sides known: the most area is at $90^\circ$
tips.text: **When:** you know two sides, $a$ and $b$, but not the angle between them. **Then:** the area is biggest when that angle is $90^\circ$, and that biggest area is $\frac12ab$. Any other angle squashes the triangle flatter and gives less.
tips.example: Sides $6$ and $8$: the area is above $0$ and at most $\frac12\times6\times8=24$. Comparing the area with $24$? If a right angle is possible, the area could equal $24$ or be less, so the answer is (D). If it isn't possible, $24$ is bigger.

tips.title: Sides $\times k$ means area $\times k^2$
tips.text: **When:** one shape is a scaled copy of another (same angles, different size). **Then:** if the sides are $k$ times as long, the area is $k^2$ times as big and the volume $k^3$ times. Common case: a line joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle cuts off a small copy with half the sides, so a **quarter** of the area.
tips.example: A triangle has area $36$. The small triangle above the midpoint line has $\frac14\times36=9$, and the strip below it has $36-9=27$.

tips.title: Longest side faces the biggest angle
tips.text: **When:** a question asks you to order a triangle's sides or angles, or to compare two of them. **Then:** sides and angles line up in the **same order**: the longest side is across from the biggest angle, the shortest side across from the smallest, and equal sides across from equal angles. It runs both ways, so you can order the sides from the angles too.
tips.example: Sides $AB=5$, $BC=7$, $AC=9$: $AC$ is longest, so $\angle B$ (across from it) is the biggest angle, and $\angle C$ (across from $AB$) is the smallest. Backwards: if $\angle A=50^\circ$ and $\angle B=60^\circ$, then $\angle C=70^\circ$, so $BC<AC<AB$.

tips.title: Top corner hangs past the base: extend the base
tips.text: **When:** one angle at the end of the base is over $90^\circ$, so the top corner hangs out **past** that end. **Then:** the height must still meet the base at a right angle, so **extend the base line** past that end and drop the height onto the extension. The height lands **outside** the triangle. The area is still $\frac12\times$ base $\times$ height, using the original base, not the extended one.
tips.example: Base from $(0,0)$ to $(10,0)$, top corner at $(-2.6,\,16.8)$. Extend the base left to $(-2.6,\,0)$: the height is $16.8$, so the area is $\frac12\times10\times16.8=84$. The extra $2.6$ is not part of the base.

sections.title: Lines & graphs
sections.idea: Slope just means 'how far **up** for each step **right**'. Most line questions come down to slope.

example.q: A line goes through $(1, 6)$ and is perpendicular to a line with slope $\frac23$. Where does it cross the $x$-axis?
steps: Perpendicular slope: flip the fraction and change the sign. $\frac23\to-\frac32$.
$-\frac32$ means every 2 steps right, the line drops 3.
To get from $y=6$ down to $y=0$ it drops 6. That takes $2\times2=4$ steps right.
$x=1+4=5$, so it crosses at $(5, 0)$.

facts: **Quadrants** are numbered I to IV **counterclockwise**, starting top right: I is $(+,+)$, II is $(-,+)$, III is $(-,-)$, IV is $(+,-)$. A point on an axis is in no quadrant.
Slope $=\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.
For a line written as $Ax+By=C$, the slope is $-\frac AB$.
**Perpendicular** lines (meeting at a right angle): flip the fraction **and** change the sign.
**Parallel** lines have the **same** slope.

**Line from a slope and a point:** if you know the slope $m$ and one point $(x_0,y_0)$, the line is $y-y_0=m(x-x_0)$. So a line through $(x_0,y_0)$ **perpendicular** to $Ax+By+C=0$ (slope $-\frac AB$) is $y-y_0=\frac BA(x-x_0)$. Example: through $(1,6)$, perpendicular to $2x-3y=5$: slope $-\frac32$, so $y-6=-\frac32(x-1)$.
Crossing the $x$-axis means $y=0$. Crossing the $y$-axis means $x=0$.

**Line from its two intercepts:** a line crossing the $x$-axis at $(p,0)$ and the $y$-axis at $(0,q)$ is $\frac xp+\frac yq=1$, with slope $-\frac qp$. Read the intercepts straight off: $\frac x4+\frac y6=1$ crosses at $(4,0)$ and $(0,6)$. To get this form from $Ax+By=C$, divide both sides by $C$: $3x+2y=12$ becomes $\frac x4+\frac y6=1$. The triangle it cuts off with the axes has area $\frac12|pq|$.
Midpoint: average the $x$'s, average the $y$'s.
**Distance from a point to a line:** for the point $(x_0,y_0)$ and the line $Ax+By+C=0$, $d=\frac{|Ax_0+By_0+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}$. Example: from $(1,2)$ to $3x+4y-1=0$ is $\frac{|3+8-1|}{5}=2$.
tricks: Sketch it quickly. Answers on the wrong side of an axis can be crossed off right away.

Square from two opposite corners: find the midpoint. Walk from it to one corner (say 3 right, 2 up). Turn that walk a quarter turn (2 left, 3 up) and walk it from the midpoint to reach another corner.
traps: Changing the sign but forgetting to flip the fraction, or flipping it without changing the sign.
Answering where the line crosses the $y$-axis when they asked about the $x$-axis.
Calling a rectangle a square without checking that its sides are equal.
Plugging into the point-to-line formula before moving everything to one side. $3x+4y=1$ must become $3x+4y-1=0$, so $C=-1$, not $1$.
Numbering the quadrants clockwise. II is top **left** and IV is bottom **right**.

tips.title: Name the quadrant from the signs
tips.text: **When:** a question says a point or a line is in, or passes through, a quadrant. **Do:** start at the top right (I) and go **counterclockwise**, the way the arrow turns: I $(+,+)$, II $(-,+)$, III $(-,-)$, IV $(+,-)$. The $x$ sign is the side (right is $+$), the $y$ sign is up or down (up is $+$).
tips.example: $(-3, 5)$: $x$ is negative (left), $y$ is positive (up), so quadrant II. $(4,-1)$ is quadrant IV.

tips.title: Find where the line crosses each axis
tips.text: **When:** a line and the two axes make a triangle. **Do:** set $y=0$ to find where it crosses the $x$-axis (call it $a$), and set $x=0$ to find where it crosses the $y$-axis (call it $b$). The triangle has a right angle at the origin, so its area is $\frac12ab$ (use the lengths, ignore minus signs). Going the other way, the line through those two points is $\frac xa+\frac yb=1$.
tips.example: $3x+4y=24$. Set $y=0$: $x=8$. Set $x=0$: $y=6$. Triangle area $=\frac12\times8\times6=24$.

tips.title: Shoelace formula: area straight from the corners
tips.text: **When:** you know every corner of a shape as $(x,y)$ points and it isn't a neat rectangle or right triangle. It works for **any polygon** with $n$ corners (a triangle needs 3 points, a quadrilateral 4, a pentagon 5) as long as (1) every edge is **straight**, so no circles or arcs, and (2) the edges **don't cross** each other (no bowtie or figure-8). **Do:** list the corners in order around the edge, all clockwise or all counterclockwise, never skipping across. Then $A=\frac12\left|(x_1y_2-y_1x_2)+(x_2y_3-y_2x_3)+\dots+(x_ny_1-y_nx_1)\right|$: each pair is one corner times the next, cross-multiplied, and the last pair wraps back to the first corner. The absolute value means direction doesn't matter. For a quadrilateral that is $A=\frac12\left|(x_1y_2-y_1x_2)+(x_2y_3-y_2x_3)+(x_3y_4-y_3x_4)+(x_4y_1-y_4x_1)\right|$. **Shortcut:** a triangle with one corner at $(0,0)$ and the others at $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ has area $\frac12|x_1y_2-y_1x_2|$.
tips.example: Corners $(1,0),(4,1),(3,4),(0,2)$ in order: $(1\cdot1-0\cdot4)+(4\cdot4-1\cdot3)+(3\cdot2-4\cdot0)+(0\cdot0-2\cdot1)=1+13+6-2=18$, so the area is $\frac12\times18=9$. Triangle $(0,0),(6,2),(1,5)$: $\frac12|6\cdot5-2\cdot1|=\frac12\times28=14$. Listing the quadrilateral as $(1,0),(3,4),(4,1),(0,2)$ crosses its own edges and gives the wrong area.

sections.title: Polygons, area & volume
sections.idea: Walk all the way around any shape and you turn one full circle, so the outside angles **always add up to $360^\circ$**. That one fact solves most polygon angle questions.

example.q: Each inside angle of a regular polygon is $140^\circ$. How many diagonals does it have?
steps: Inside + outside angle make a straight line, so the outside angle is $180-140=40^\circ$.
All outside angles add to $360^\circ$, so it has $\frac{360}{40}=9$ sides.
Diagonals $=\frac{9\times(9-3)}{2}=\frac{54}{2}=27$.

facts: Outside angles add to $360^\circ$. In a regular shape (all sides equal), each one is $\frac{360}{n}$.
Inside angle + outside angle $=180^\circ$.
All inside angles add to $(n-2)\times180^\circ$: triangle 180, square 360, pentagon 540.
Diagonals $=\frac{n(n-3)}{2}$. Each corner connects to $n-3$ others, and every diagonal gets counted twice.
Rectangles with the same diagonal: the **square** has the biggest perimeter. The skinnier the rectangle, the smaller the perimeter.

Trapezoid (one pair of parallel sides, the **bases**): area $=\frac{b_1+b_2}{2}\times h$, the average base times the height. The height is the straight-up distance between the bases, never a slanted side.
Box volume = length × width × height. Cylinder volume $=\pi r^2\times$ height.
tricks: 'Inside angle is 5 times the outside angle': outside + 5 × outside $=180$, so outside $=30^\circ$ and there are $\frac{360}{30}=12$ sides.
'Which could be' questions: find the **smallest and largest** possible values first, then check each choice.
traps: Assuming the sides are whole numbers when the question never says so.
Giving the number of sides when they asked for diagonals.
Forgetting to divide $n(n-3)$ by 2.
Using a trapezoid's slanted side as its height. Drop a straight-down line from the top base instead.

tips.title: The closer to a square, the better
tips.text: **Same perimeter:** the more square-like the rectangle, the **bigger** its area. **Same area:** the square has the **smallest** perimeter. Long, thin rectangles are the other extreme.
tips.example: Area $36$: a $6\times6$ square has perimeter $24$, a $9\times4$ rectangle has $26$, and a $12\times3$ one has $30$.

tips.title: The longest stick that fits in a box
tips.text: **When:** they ask for the distance from one corner of a box, through the inside, to the opposite corner (the longest stick that fits). **Do:** use Pythagoras with all three sides: $d=\sqrt{l^2+w^2+h^2}$. For a cube with side $s$, that's $s\sqrt3$.
tips.example: A $3\times4\times12$ box: $d=\sqrt{9+16+144}=\sqrt{169}=13$.

tips.title: A trapezoid is its middle line times its height
tips.text: **The midsegment** joins the midpoints of the two slanted sides. It is always parallel to the bases, and its length is exactly their average: $\text{midsegment}=\frac{b_1+b_2}{2}$. So the area is simply **midsegment × height**: the trapezoid has the same area as a rectangle that wide.
tips.example: Bases $6$ and $14$, height $5$: the midsegment is $\frac{6+14}{2}=10$, so the area is $10\times5=50$. Told the midsegment is $9$ and the area is $36$? Then $h=\frac{36}{9}=4$, without ever finding the bases.

tips.title: Diagonals cut a trapezoid into four triangles
tips.text: Call the diagonals' crossing point $E$. **Top and bottom** ($\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle CDE$) are similar, scaled by $k=\frac{AB}{CD}=\frac{BE}{ED}$, so their areas are in the ratio $k^2$. **A side triangle and the top** ($\triangle ADE$ and $\triangle ABE$) share the same height from $A$ down to $BD$, so their areas are in the ratio of their bases: $\frac{\text{Area}(\triangle ABE)}{\text{Area}(\triangle ADE)}=\frac{BE}{ED}=k$. Put together, with bases $a$ (top) and $b$ (bottom), the four areas run $a^2 : ab : ab : b^2$. **Shortcut:** if the top and bottom triangles have areas $A_1$ and $A_2$, each side triangle is $\sqrt{A_1A_2}$ (the two side triangles are always equal), and the whole trapezoid is $(\sqrt{A_1}+\sqrt{A_2})^2$.
tips.example: Top triangle $9$, bottom triangle $36$. Each side triangle is $\sqrt{9\times36}=18$, and the total is $(\sqrt9+\sqrt{36})^2=(3+6)^2=81$. Check: $9+18+18+36=81$. The bases are in the ratio $\sqrt9:\sqrt{36}=1:2$.

tips.title: Isosceles trapezoid: drop two heights
tips.text: **When:** the two slanted sides are equal and you need the height (or a slanted side). **Do:** drop a height from each top corner. That leaves a rectangle in the middle and two matching right triangles at the ends, each with base $\frac{b_2-b_1}{2}$ (the overhang). Then Pythagoras finishes it, and 3-4-5 / 6-8-10 triangles show up often.
tips.example: Bases $10$ and $22$, slanted sides $10$: each overhang is $\frac{22-10}{2}=6$, so $h=\sqrt{10^2-6^2}=8$ and the area is $\frac{10+22}{2}\times8=128$.

sections.title: Counting & probability
sections.idea: Counting is **filling slots**. Count the choices for each slot and multiply, and always fill the **pickiest** slot first.

example.q: In how many ways can 5 people stand in a line if Sam and Tia must stand next to each other?
steps: Tape Sam and Tia together into one block. Now you're lining up 4 things: $4!=24$ ways.
Inside the block they can be Sam-Tia or Tia-Sam: $\times2$.
$24\times2=48$ ways.

facts: Lining up $n$ different things: $n!$ ways ($4!=4\times3\times2\times1=24$).
Picking a group where order doesn't matter: $\binom nk$, read '$n$ choose $k$'. $\binom52=10$.
Some things the same? Divide out the repeats: AABB has $\frac{4!}{2!\,2!}=6$ orders.
**Must be together:** tape them into a block, line up the blocks, then $\times2$ because the two can swap.
**Must NOT be together:** all the ways − the ways they're together.
Probability $=\frac{\text{good outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes}}$. P(at least one) $=1-$ P(none).
tricks: **Pickiest first.** If Ann can't sit at either end of 8 seats, give Ann her 6 choices before anyone else sits.
If one person's choice changes how many choices the next person has, split it into cases, or count the opposite and subtract.
'Digits in decreasing order' means the order is already decided. You're only **choosing** the digits, so use $\binom nk$.
Not sure? Try a tiny version (3 people) and list every possibility to check your method.
traps: Multiplying as if the choices don't affect each other when they do.
Forgetting the $\times2$ for the two people in a block swapping places.
In 'none of A, B or C' problems, subtracting the overlaps but forgetting to add the triple overlap back.

tips.title: Every order is equally likely
tips.text: **When:** people line up at random and the question is about the order of a few named people. **Then:** skip the counting. Every order of those people is equally likely, so A is ahead of B in exactly **half** of all line-ups. Three named people can come in $3!=6$ orders, so any one order (A, then B, then C) has chance $\frac16$.
tips.example: 6 people line up at random. P(Ann is somewhere ahead of Bo) $=\frac12$.

tips.title: Every pair once: $\binom n2$
tips.text: **When:** each thing is paired with every other thing exactly once: handshakes, every team playing every other team once, lines through $n$ points (no three on one line). **Do:** count the pairs, $\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2$.
tips.example: 10 teams, each playing every other team once: $\frac{10\times9}{2}=45$ games. If they play each other twice: $90$.

tips.title: The 4th draw is just like the 1st
tips.text: **When:** items are drawn one at a time without being put back, and you are **not told** what came out earlier. **Then:** any single draw (the 2nd, the 4th, the last) has the same chance as the first draw. No probability tree needed.
tips.example: A box has 3 gold and 7 silver coins, drawn one at a time without putting them back. P(the 4th coin is gold) = P(the 1st coin is gold) $=\frac3{10}$. This only works because you know nothing about draws 1 to 3.

patterns.title: Stars and bars: identical things into groups
patterns.idea: To share $n$ **identical** things among $k$ groups (a group may get none), picture $n$ stars in a row and $k-1$ dividers placed among them. Each arrangement is one way to share, so there are $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$ ways. The cases below are this same method in different disguises.

cases.name: Identical items to people, zero allowed
cases.q: In how many ways can 10 identical cookies go to 4 children if a child may get none?
cases.spot: 'identical' or 'indistinguishable' items, and 'may receive none'.
steps: $n=10$ cookies (stars), $k=4$ children (groups).

cases.name: At least one each
cases.q: Same 10 cookies and 4 children, but each child gets at least one.
cases.spot: 'at least one', 'no group is empty', 'positive integers'.
steps: Hand 1 cookie to each child first: $10-4=6$ left.

cases.name: Different minimums
cases.q: How many integer solutions does $x+y+z=15$ have with $x\ge2$, $y\ge3$, $z\ge0$?
cases.spot: an equation adding up to a total, with $\ge$ limits under it.
steps: Pay the minimums first: $15-2-3-0=10$ left.

cases.name: Menu or store choice (repeats allowed)
cases.q: A shop sells 4 kinds of flower. How many different bouquets of 7 flowers can you make?
cases.spot: picking $n$ things from $k$ kinds, order doesn't matter, repeats allowed.
steps: The kinds are the groups ($k=4$); the picks are the stars ($n=7$).

cases.name: Digit sum of 9 or less
cases.q: How many 4-digit positive integers have digits that add up to 7?
cases.spot: 'sum of the digits' with a target of 9 or less, so no digit can go over 9.
steps: Put 1 in the thousands place so it can't be 0: $7-1=6$ left.
Now $n=6$, $k=4$ digit slots: $\binom{9}{3}=\mathbf{84}$.

cases.name: Ordered factorization
cases.q: How many ordered triples $(a,b,c)$ of positive integers have $abc=72$?
cases.spot: 'ordered' triples (or pairs, quadruples) multiplying to a number.
steps: $72=2^3\times3^2$. Each prime's copies are identical stars; $a$, $b$, $c$ are the 3 groups.
Three 2s into 3 groups: $\binom{5}{2}=10$. Two 3s into 3 groups: $\binom{4}{2}=6$.
Multiply: $10\times6=\mathbf{60}$.

cases.name: Digit sum just over 9: subtract the overflows
cases.q: How many 3-digit numbers have digits that add up to 11?
cases.spot: a digit sum of 10 or more, so one digit could wrongly reach 10.
steps: Give the hundreds digit 1 first (it can't be 0). That leaves 10 to share over 3 digits: $\binom{12}{2}=66$ ways.
Some of those give one digit 10 or more, which isn't a digit. Take them out.
Hundreds too big: it already has 1, so give it 9 more, leaving 1: $\binom{3}{2}=3$ bad ways. Tens too big: give it 10, leaving 0: $1$ bad way. Ones: also $1$.

cases.name: Digit sum near the max: count down from 999
cases.q: How many 3-digit numbers have digits that add up to 24?
cases.spot: a digit sum close to the largest possible ($27$ for 3 digits).
steps: Start at 999 (digit sum 27) and take away $27-24=3$ in total, spread over the digits.
Taking away only 3 can't push any digit below 0 or turn the first digit into 0, so nothing needs to be ruled out.
Share 3 'take-aways' among 3 digits: $\binom{5}{2}=\mathbf{10}$.

notWhen: **Different** items: 10 different books to 4 children is $4^{10}$ (each book picks a child).
**Unordered** factorizations ('sets of 3 integers whose product is 72'): list them by hand.
**Product** of digits ('4-digit numbers whose digits multiply to 24'): list the digit sets, then count each set's orders with $\frac{4!}{\text{repeats}!}$.

sections.title: Overlapping groups & max/min
sections.idea: When people are in two groups, the ones in **both** get counted twice. Every group formula is just fixing that double count.

example.q: Of 40 students, 25 play soccer and 22 play basketball. What is the fewest number who could play both?
steps: $25+22=47$, but there are only 40 students.
So at least $47-40=7$ students were counted twice.
The fewest who play both is **7** (that's when every student plays at least one).

facts: Total $=A+B-$ both $+$ neither.
Exactly one group $=A+B-2\times$ both. (Take the 'both' people out of each group.)
'Both' can't be bigger than the smaller group, and can't be smaller than $A+B-$ total.
tricks: Max or min question? First find the smallest and biggest possible 'both', then plug those in.
Draw a 2×2 table (in A / not in A by in B / not in B). Fill what you know; the rest falls out.
To make one thing as **big** as possible, make everything else as **small** as allowed.
traps: Assuming nobody is in both groups when the numbers don't allow it.
Assuming everyone is in at least one group.
In 'which could be' questions, checking odd/even but forgetting the smallest and largest limits.

tips.title: Three groups: undo the double counting
tips.text: **Why it's tricky:** adding $A+B+C$ counts a person in two groups **twice** and a person in all three **three times**. **If you know how many are in exactly two:** Total $=A+B+C-(\text{exactly two})-2(\text{all three})+\text{neither}$. **If you know the pair overlaps** $AB$, $AC$, $BC$ (each already includes the all-three people): Total $=A+B+C-(AB+AC+BC)+ABC+\text{neither}$.
tips.example: Clubs of 20, 25 and 30; 60 students, each in at least one club; 9 in exactly two. Call the all-three count $x$: $75-9-2x=60$, so $x=3$.

tips.title: 'Guarantee' means plan for the worst luck
tips.text: **When:** they ask for the fewest picks that **guarantee** something. **Do:** imagine the unluckiest picks possible: take as many as you can *without* getting what you want. Then add **1**. To guarantee $k$ of the same kind when there are $n$ kinds: $n(k-1)+1$. If a kind has fewer than $k-1$ items, you can only take what it has.
tips.example: A drawer has 10 red, 8 blue and 6 green socks, and you pick in the dark. Fewest socks to guarantee 3 of one colour? Worst luck: 2 red, 2 blue, 2 green, which is 6 socks and no three alike. The **7th** sock must make a three, so the answer is $7$.

sections.title: Remainders, factors & powers
sections.idea: Remainders and last digits **repeat in a pattern**. Find the pattern with the first few powers, and you never have to work out a huge number.

example.q: What is the last digit of $7^{43}$?
steps: Last digits of $7^1, 7^2, 7^3, 7^4$: 7, 9, 3, 1. Then it starts over, so the pattern repeats every 4.
$43=40+3$. The 40 is ten full rounds, so we land on the **3rd** spot.
The 3rd spot is **3**.

facts: When you want a remainder, you can swap any number for its own remainder first. $17\div8$ leaves 1, so $17^{50}\div8$ leaves $1^{50}=1$.
Last digits repeat: 2, 3, 7, 8 every 4 powers; 4 and 9 every 2; 0, 1, 5, 6 never change.
**Each number has its own pattern length.** Don't assume two bases repeat at the same speed.
Any odd number squared leaves remainder 1 when divided by 8 ($9$, $25$, $49$…).
Only perfect squares have an odd number of factors.
tricks: Write out the first few remainders until they repeat, then jump ahead using the pattern length.
'$k$ leaves remainder 5 when divided by 6'? Test real numbers: $k=5$, then $k=11$.
Comparing factor counts? Test 1, a prime, a prime power **and** a number made of several primes, like 30.
traps: Assuming two different bases repeat at the same speed.
Testing only primes and missing the case that flips the answer.

tips.title: Counting positive divisors
tips.text: **Do:** break $n$ into primes, $n=p^a\times q^b\times\ldots$ Add 1 to each exponent and multiply: the count is $(a+1)(b+1)\cdots$ It counts 1 and $n$ too. Each divisor picks how many of each prime to use, from 0 up to its exponent, which is why every exponent gets $+1$.
tips.example: $36=2^2\times3^2$, so $(2+1)\times(2+1)=3\times3=\mathbf{9}$ divisors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. $12=2^2\times3^1$ has $3\times2=6$. A prime $p$ alone has $1+1=2$.

tips.title: How many times a prime goes into $n!$ (and zeros at the end)
tips.text: **Do:** divide $n$ by $p$, then by $p^2$, then by $p^3$, and so on. Drop the decimals each time and add up the results. **Zeros at the end** of $n!$ each come from a $2\times5$ pair. There are always fewer 5s than 2s, so just count the 5s.
tips.example: Zeros at the end of $50!$: $\frac{50}{5}=10$ and $\frac{50}{25}=2$, so $12$ zeros. Largest $k$ with $3^k$ dividing $20!$: $\frac{20}{3}\to6$ and $\frac{20}{9}\to2$, so $k=8$.

tips.title: Same remainder, or the same amount short
tips.text: **Same remainder every time:** if $n$ leaves remainder $r$ for several divisors, then $n$ = a multiple of their LCM (the smallest number they all divide into), plus $r$. **Same amount short every time:** if each remainder is the same amount less than its divisor, then $n$ = a multiple of the LCM, minus that amount.
tips.example: Remainder 2 when divided by 3, 4 and 5: the LCM is 60, so $n=60k+2$, giving $2, 62, 122, \ldots$ Remainder 2 when divided by 3 and 3 when divided by 4: each is 1 short, the LCM is 12, so $n=12k-1$, giving $11, 23, 35, \ldots$

tips.title: Adding powers: pull out the smallest
tips.text: **Rule:** you can't combine exponents across a $+$ or $-$ ($2^3+2^4$ is **not** $2^7$). **Do:** factor out the smallest power, then work out what's left. Equal powers just stack: $2^n+2^n=2\times2^n=2^{n+1}$.

patterns.title: Far-off terms: find the cycle, or cancel
patterns.idea: Asked for the 50th term, the 100th digit or a sum of 99 terms? Look at the formula first. If each term is built **only from the term before it** (no $k$ anywhere), the values must loop: write terms until one repeats, then jump ahead with the remainder. If **$k$ itself sits in a denominator**, the terms never loop; split each one into two fractions and watch the middle of the sum cancel.

cases.name: Term built only from the one before
cases.q: $t_1=2$ and $t_{k+1}=\frac{t_k-1}{t_k+1}$ for $k\ge1$. What is $t_{50}$?
cases.spot: the rule uses $t_k$ but never $k$ itself, often inside a fraction.
steps: Write terms: $t_1=2$, $t_2=\frac13$, $t_3=-\frac12$, $t_4=-3$, $t_5=2$. Back to the start, so the cycle is 4 long.
$50=(4\times12)+\mathbf{2}$. Twelve full loops, then 2 more steps.
Remainder 2 means the 2nd spot: $t_{50}=t_2=\mathbf{\tfrac13}$.

cases.name: Sum that skips terms
cases.q: Same sequence. What is $t_3+t_6+t_9+\cdots+t_{60}$?
cases.spot: only every 2nd, 3rd... term is added, so the picks step through the cycle unevenly.
steps: The picks move 3 places each time through a cycle of 4. Since $\gcd(3,4)=1$, they land on all 4 spots before repeating: $t_3, t_2, t_1, t_4$, then again.
So every 4 picks add up to one whole cycle: $2+\frac13-\frac12-3=-\frac76$.
$t_3$ to $t_{60}$ is $\frac{60}{3}=20$ picks, which is $\frac{20}{4}=5$ full rounds: $5\times(-\frac76)=\mathbf{-\tfrac{35}{6}}$.
If the gcd were bigger (step 2 through a cycle of 4), the picks would land on only $\frac42=2$ of the spots, and a round would be just those.

cases.name: Repeating decimal with a late start
cases.q: What is the sum of the 100th, 101st and 102nd digits after the decimal point of $\frac{5}{28}$?
cases.spot: a far-off digit of a fraction whose denominator has a 2 or 5 in it, so some digits come before the loop.
steps: Divide carefully: $\frac{5}{28}=0.17857142857\ldots=0.17\overline{857142}$. The **17** never repeats (2 digits); the block **857142** is 6 long.
Skip the 2 lead-in digits: the 100th digit is the $100-2=98$th digit of the block.
$98=(6\times16)+\mathbf{2}$, so the 100th, 101st and 102nd digits are the block's 2nd, 3rd and 4th: 5, 7 and 1.

cases.name: $k$ in the denominator: split and cancel
cases.q: What is $\frac{1}{1\cdot2}+\frac{1}{2\cdot3}+\frac{1}{3\cdot4}+\cdots+\frac{1}{99\cdot100}$?
cases.spot: each term is $\frac{1}{k(k+1)}$ or similar: $k$ is in the formula, so nothing loops.
steps: Split each term: $\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\frac1k-\frac{1}{k+1}$.
Write it out: $(1-\frac12)+(\frac12-\frac13)+\cdots+(\frac{1}{99}-\frac{1}{100})$. Every middle piece cancels with its neighbour.
Only the first and last survive: $1-\frac{1}{100}=\mathbf{\tfrac{99}{100}}$.

notWhen: **Remainder 0** isn't 'before the start': it means the **last** spot of the cycle ($t_{48}=t_4=-3$ above).
Gaps of 2 apart ($\frac{1}{k(k+2)}$) still cancel, but $\frac{1}{k(k+2)}=\frac12\left(\frac1k-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)$: keep the $\frac12$, and **two** pieces survive at each end.

sections.title: Algebra & inequalities
sections.idea: An inequality works like an equation with **one extra rule**: multiply or divide by a negative and you must flip the sign.

steps: $|x-1|$ is the distance from $x$ to 1, so this says: distance to 1 + distance to 5 is at most 6.
Anywhere between 1 and 5 the total is 4. Each step outside adds 2.
So you can go 1 step past each end: $0\le x\le6$.

facts: Multiply or divide by a negative → **flip** the $<$ or $>$.
$(x-a)(x-b)<0$ (with $a<b$) holds only **between** $a$ and $b$. With $>0$, it holds **outside** them.
$|x-a|$ means 'how far $x$ is from $a$ on the number line'.
If $x+\frac1x=s$, squaring both sides gives $x^2+\frac1{x^2}=s^2-2$.
For $x^2+bx+c=0$, the two answers **add** to $-b$ and **multiply** to $c$.
Two lines with the same slope never meet: **no solution**. If they're the exact same line: **infinitely many**.
tricks: Two inequalities at once? Solve each, draw both on a number line, and keep the overlap.
Getting $k^2=36$? Try **both** $6$ and $-6$ back in the question.
Can't solve it? Plug in the answer choices.
traps: Forgetting to flip the sign.
Using an endpoint that isn't allowed. With $<$, the endpoint itself is out.
Choosing the value that makes the two lines the **same** when they asked for 'no solution'.
Sign mix-up: the answers add to $-b$, not $b$.

tips.title: Don't solve for each letter
tips.text: **When:** they ask for a combination like $x+y$ or $4x+4y$, not $x$ and $y$ on their own. **Do:** add or subtract the whole equations first. Often the combination appears right away.
tips.example: $3x+2y=14$ and $x+2y=6$. Add them: $4x+4y=20$, so $x+y=5$. You never needed $x$ or $y$.

tips.title: Spot $a^2-b^2$ in disguise
tips.text: $a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$. **Look for it** when one square is subtracted from another, or when two numbers being multiplied sit the same distance either side of a round number.

tips.title: Given $a+b$ and $ab$? Don't find $a$ and $b$
tips.text: **When:** the question gives you $a+b$ and $ab$. **Do:** use these two lines instead of solving: $a^2+b^2=(a+b)^2-2ab$ and $(a-b)^2=(a+b)^2-4ab$.

tips.title: Sum and product of the solutions, without solving
tips.text: **When:** they ask about the two solutions (roots) of $ax^2+bx+c=0$, but don't need the roots themselves. **Do:** read them off the equation. The roots **add** to $-\frac ba$ and **multiply** to $\frac ca$. Then rewrite what they ask for using the sum and product, like $\frac1p+\frac1q=\frac{p+q}{pq}$.
tips.example: $p$ and $q$ solve $2x^2-7x+4=0$. Find $\frac1p+\frac1q$. Here $a=2$, $b=-7$, $c=4$, so $p+q=\frac72$ and $pq=\frac42=2$. Then $\frac{p+q}{pq}=\frac{7/2}{2}=\frac74$. No messy square roots.

sections.title: Ratios, percents & word problems
sections.idea: Find the thing that **doesn't change** and build your equation around it.

example.q: A club's ratio of boys to girls is $2:3$. After 10 boys join, the ratio is $1:1$. How many people were in the club before?
steps: The girls don't change. Call them $3k$; the boys were $2k$.
After: boys $2k+10$ = girls $3k$, so $k=10$.
Before: $2k+3k=5k=$ **50** people. (They asked for 'before', not after.)

facts: A ratio of $3:5$ means the amounts are $3k$ and $5k$. The total, $8k$, is a multiple of 8.
Joining two ratios: make the shared item match. A:B $=2:3$ and B:C $=4:5$. Make B 12: A:B:C $=8:12:15$.
'X is what percent **more than** Y': divide the difference by Y, the number after 'than'.
Up $p\%$ means multiply by $1+\frac p{100}$. Up 25% = $\times1.25$. Up 700% = $\times8$, **not** $\times7$.
Growing the same percent every year means **multiplying** by the same number every year. $\times8$ over 3 periods is $\times2$ each time, because $2\times2\times2=8$.
Working together: **add the rates**. A takes 3 hours ($\frac13$ of the job per hour) and B takes 6 ($\frac16$ per hour). Together: $\frac13+\frac16=\frac12$ per hour, so 2 hours.
tricks: Let one letter stand for the smallest amount and write everything else using it.
Before you answer, reread the last sentence and **underline what they're asking for**.
Plug your answer back into the story to check.
traps: Giving a middle step (one person's share) instead of what they asked for (the total).
Splitting growth evenly: up 700% over 3 periods is **not** 233% each time.
Dividing by the wrong number in 'percent more than' questions.
In a 'when I was your age' puzzle, splitting the two given ages into **2** gaps. There are four ages on the line, so **3** gaps.

tips.title: $x\%$ of $y$ = $y\%$ of $x$
tips.text: A percent works either way round, so swap the two numbers when the other way is easier.
tips.example: $16\%$ of $25$ is hard; $25\%$ of $16$ is a quarter of 16, which is $4$.

tips.title: Average speed isn't the average of the speeds
tips.text: **Rule:** average speed = total distance ÷ total time. **Shortcut:** for the same distance at speeds $a$ and $b$, the average speed is $\frac{2ab}{a+b}$. It's always below the plain average $\frac{a+b}2$, because you spend more time at the slower speed.
tips.example: 60 mph there and 40 mph back: $\frac{2\times60\times40}{60+40}=\frac{4800}{100}=48$ mph, not 50.

tips.title: "When I was your age": four ages, three equal gaps
tips.text: **When:** a puzzle says 'when A was as old as B is now…' and 'when B is as old as A is now…'. **Do:** skip the equations. The age gap between two people never changes, and each jump back or forward in the story is exactly that gap. So the four ages in the story sit **equally spaced** on one line: younger then, younger now (= older then), older now (= younger later), older later. The first and last are given, so split the distance between them into **3** equal gaps, not 2.
tips.example: When Ana was as old as Ben is now, Ben was 6. When Ben is as old as Ana is now, Ana will be 33. Gap: $\frac{33-6}{3}=9$. So Ben is $6+9=$ **15** and Ana is $15+9=$ **24**. Check: 9 years ago Ana was 15 and Ben was 6; in 9 years Ben is 24 and Ana is 33.

patterns.title: Two swimmers, second meeting
patterns.idea: Two swimmers start at the same moment from opposite ends of a $50$ m pool and turn at each wall. The **first** meeting is always head-on, at $t=\frac{50}{v_f+v_s}$. For the **second** meeting, divide the faster speed by the slower one **before anything else**. Under 2: they cross head-on again, after covering $150$ m between them. Exactly 2: they arrive at the same wall together. Over 2: the fast swimmer turns and catches the slow one from behind, once it is $50$ m further along than the slow one.

cases.name: Ratio under 2: second head-on crossing
cases.q: A swims at $1.25$ m/s from the 0 m wall, B at $1$ m/s from the 50 m wall. When do they meet for the second time?
cases.spot: $\frac{v_f}{v_s}<2$: both swimmers turn before they meet again.
steps: Ratio $1.25<2$, so they meet head-on, with $150$ m covered between them (one length to the first meeting, two more to the second).
$t=\frac{150}{1.25+1}=\frac{150}{2.25}=\mathbf{66.67}$ **s**. Check: A has swum $83.3$ m and B $66.7$ m, so both are at the $16.7$ m mark.

cases.name: Ratio exactly 2: tie at the wall
cases.q: A swims at $2$ m/s from the 0 m wall, B at $1$ m/s from the 50 m wall. When and where do they meet for the second time?
cases.spot: $\frac{v_f}{v_s}=2$: both formulas give the same time.
steps: First meeting: $t=\frac{50}{3}=16.67$ s, at the $33.3$ m mark.
Second: $t=\frac{50}{v_s}=\mathbf{50}$ **s**. A has swum $100$ m (there and back) and B $50$ m (one length), so both reach the **0 m wall** at the same instant.
$\frac{150}{2+1}=50$ and $\frac{50}{2-1}=50$: the two rules agree.

cases.name: Ratio over 2: overtake from behind
cases.q: A swims at $3$ m/s from the 0 m wall, B at $1$ m/s from the 50 m wall. When and where do they meet for the second time?
cases.spot: $\frac{v_f}{v_s}>2$: the fast swimmer turns and laps the slow one before the slow one reaches a wall.
steps: First meeting: $t=\frac{50}{4}=12.5$ s, at the $37.5$ m mark.
A turns at the 50 m wall at $t=16.67$ s. B is still heading for 0 m, at the $33.3$ m mark.
A catches B once A has swum $50$ m more than B: $t=\frac{50}{3-1}=\mathbf{25}$ **s**. A has swum $75$ m and B $25$ m, so they meet at the **25 m mark**.

sections.title: Averages, spread & charts
sections.idea: When you combine groups, **group size matters**: a big group pulls the average toward itself.

example.q: Class A has 10 students averaging 80. Class B has 30 students averaging 60. What is the average of all 40?
steps: Totals: $10\times80=800$ and $30\times60=1800$.
Not 70! The bigger class pulls the average toward 60.

facts: Combining groups: add all the totals, then divide by everyone. Don't just average the averages.
Bell curve: about 68% are within 1 standard deviation (SD) of the middle, and 95% within 2.
So about **16%** are more than 1 SD **above** the middle, and about **2.5%** are more than 2 SD above.
A z-score counts SDs from the mean: $z=\frac{x-\text{mean}}{\text{SD}}$. Compare values from two bell curves by their z-scores.
Expected value of a random variable: multiply each value by its probability, then add.
SD measures how spread out the numbers are. Add the same amount to every number and the spread stays the same.
Median = the middle number once they're sorted. With an even count, average the two middle ones.
Q1 = middle of the lower half, Q3 = middle of the upper half. IQR = Q3 − Q1.
Density curve: probability = **area** under the curve between the two values. The whole area is $1$.
tricks: Two groups with different SDs? For each group, count how many of *its own* SDs the cutoff is from its mean.
Charts: read the title, labels and units first. Estimate before you calculate.
Density questions: sketch the shape, shade the region, and use rectangles and triangles. For a slice in the middle, take $1$ minus the tails.
traps: Averaging the averages.
Using 32% (both tails of the curve) when they only asked about one side.
Thinking that adding very big or very small numbers can't move the quartiles. They change how many numbers are in each half, so the middle of each half moves.
Reading the **height** of a density as a probability. Only area is probability, and a height can be bigger than 1.
Putting the median of a lopsided density at the middle of its range. It moves toward the tall side.

tips.title: What changes the SD (the spread)
tips.text: **Add or subtract** the same number from every value: the SD stays the same (everything just slides along). **Multiply** every value by $k$: the SD and the range are multiplied by $k$ (ignore any minus sign, because spread is never negative). **Add a new value equal to the mean:** the mean stays the same, but the SD gets **smaller**.
tips.example: $\{2,4,6\}$ and $\{102,104,106\}$ have the same SD. $\{6,12,18\}$ is $\{2,4,6\}$ times 3, so its SD is 3 times as big.

tips.title: A weighted average is a see-saw
tips.text: The combined average lands between the two group averages, **closer to the bigger group**. To find the group sizes: measure how far each group's average is from the combined average, then **swap** those distances. The group farther away is the smaller one.
tips.example: Boys average 60, girls 90, the whole class 80. Boys are 20 away and girls 10 away. Swap them: boys : girls $=10:20=1:2$.

patterns.title: Probability density: probability is area
patterns.idea: For a density curve, **probability is area under the curve, never its height**, and the whole area is $1$. GRE densities are made of rectangles and straight lines, so every question turns into width $\times$ height or $\frac12\times$ base $\times$ height. **Sketch it first**, mark the region they ask about, then measure it.

cases.name: Uniform: a flat rectangle
cases.q: $X$ is uniformly distributed on $2\le x\le6$. What is $P(X>5)$?
cases.spot: 'uniformly distributed on' an interval, or 'the density is a constant $c$' on it and $0$ outside.
steps: Width $6-2=4$. Area must be $1$, so the height is $\frac14$: the top line is $y=\frac14$.
$X>5$ is the strip from $5$ to $6$: width $1$, height $\frac14$.
$P=1\times\frac14=\mathbf{\frac14}$. Shortcut: probability = (slice width) $\div$ (total width) $=\frac14$.

The region right of $\frac32$ is a right triangle: base $2-\frac32=\frac12$, height $2-\frac32=\frac12$.
Area $=\frac12\times\frac12\times\frac12=\mathbf{\frac18}$.
Shortcut: the corner is a smaller copy of the right half (area $\frac12$) with half its base, so $\left(\frac12\right)^2\times\frac12=\frac18$.

steps: Whole triangle: $\frac12\times4\times h=1$, so $h=\frac12$.
Left of the peak: base $1$, height $\frac12$, area $\frac12\times1\times\frac12=\mathbf{\frac14}$.
Shortcut: a vertical cut at the peak splits the area in the ratio of the bases, $1:3$, so the left piece is $\frac14$ without finding $h$.

cases.name: Mixed shape: split into a rectangle and a triangle
cases.q: The density of $X$ is $\frac13$ for $0\le x\le2$, then falls in a straight line to $0$ at $x=4$. What is $P(X>3)$?
cases.spot: a flat part and a sloped part, a trapezoid, or a 'step'.
steps: Check the total: rectangle $2\times\frac13=\frac23$, plus triangle $\frac12\times2\times\frac13=\frac13$. Total $1$.
The falling line goes from $(2,\frac13)$ to $(4,0)$, so at $x=3$ the height is $\frac16$.
Right of $3$: $\frac12\times1\times\frac16=\mathbf{\frac1{12}}$. Or by the corner shortcut: $\left(\frac12\right)^2\times\frac13=\frac1{12}$.

sections.title: Comparison number sense
sections.idea: In comparison questions, try to **break** the comparison. If two different numbers give different winners, the answer is (D).

steps: Try $x=\frac12$: A $=\frac14$, B $=\frac12$. B wins.
Try $x=-\frac12$: A $=\frac14$, B $=-\frac12$. A wins.
Different winners, so the answer is **(D)**.

facts: Between 0 and 1, squaring makes a number **smaller**: $\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac14$. Above 1, it makes it bigger.
For a number between 0 and 1, $\frac1x$ is bigger than 1.
$0.999\ldots$ (repeating forever) is **exactly** 1.
A repeating decimal is the repeating block over that many 9s: $0.\overline{7}=\frac79$, $0.\overline{36}=\frac{36}{99}$, $0.\overline{123}=\frac{123}{999}$.
tricks: Always try at least two numbers: $0$, $1$, $-1$, $\frac12$, a negative, a big number, and both ends of the allowed range.
Only numbers, no letters? Then it can't be (D). Just work it out.
Simplify by doing the same thing to both sides, but only multiply or divide by numbers you know are positive. A negative would swap which side is bigger.
traps: Trying only one number and stopping.
Answering in 20 seconds without trying a second number.

tips.title: Huge powers: make the exponents match
tips.text: **When:** you compare powers too big to work out, like $2^{30}$ and $3^{20}$. **Do:** rewrite both with the same exponent (or the same base), then just compare what's left.

tips.title: Powers and reciprocals: know the four zones
tips.text: **When:** the quantities are the same letter raised to different powers ($x$, $x^2$, $x^3$, $\frac1x$), or the condition is something like $x^3<x$. **Then:** the order depends on which zone $x$ is in, so find the zone first. Fractions between 0 and 1 are the usual trap: they **shrink** as the power goes up, which is backwards from whole numbers.
tips.example: $x>1$: $\frac1x<x<x^2<x^3$. $0<x<1$: $x^3<x^2<x<\frac1x$. $-1<x<0$: $\frac1x<x<x^3<x^2$. $x<-1$: $x^3<x<\frac1x<x^2$. Check any zone with one number: $2$, $\frac12$, $-\frac12$ or $-2$.

tips.title: The ZONEF checklist: test the condition first
tips.text: **When:** a letter has no clear limits. **Do:** run through **Z**ero, **O**ne ($1$ and $-1$), **N**egatives ($-2$), **E**xtremes ($100$, $-100$) and **F**ractions ($\frac12$, $-\frac12$). First throw out every number that breaks the given condition. Then plug the **survivors** into A and B. Two survivors with different winners means (D).
tips.example: $x^3<x$. Compare A: $x^2$, B: $x$. Condition: $0$, $1$, $-1$ fail ($0<0$ is false); $-2$ works ($-8<-2$); $\frac12$ works ($\frac18<\frac12$); $-\frac12$ fails ($-\frac18$ is not less than $-\frac12$). Survivors: $x=-2$ gives A $=4$, B $=-2$, so A wins. $x=\frac12$ gives A $=\frac14$, B $=\frac12$, so B wins. Answer **(D)**.

tips.title: Move everything to one side and factor
tips.text: **When:** testing numbers feels like guessing, or the condition is a power inequality. **Do:** get $0$ on one side, factor, and mark where each factor is $0$. Those points cut the number line into pieces, and the sign stays the same inside each piece. Test one number per piece (or start with $+$ on the far right and flip at each point). Now you know **every** allowed $x$, not just the ones you thought of.
tips.example: $x^3<x \Rightarrow x^3-x<0 \Rightarrow x(x-1)(x+1)<0$. The points are $-1$, $0$, $1$. Signs from right to left: $+,-,+,-$. So $x<-1$ or $0<x<1$: one piece of negatives and one piece of fractions, which is exactly why the comparison above is (D).

tips.title: Read the condition for what it really allows
tips.text: **When:** the facts look like they pin down one number. **Check:** does $x^2=16$ allow $-4$ too? Is $x$ said to be a whole number, or could it be $2.5$? Is it positive, or just 'not zero'? The square root sign means the positive root only, but solving $x^2=k$ gives two answers.
tips.example: $x^2=16$. Compare A: $x$, B: $4$. $x$ can be $4$ (equal) or $-4$ (B wins), so **(D)**. But A: $\sqrt{16}$, B: $4$ is always equal, so **(C)**.

tips.title: Pull out the shared piece
tips.text: **When:** both quantities contain the same big chunk, like a power or a long product. **Do:** divide both by it (only if it's positive) or subtract it from both, and compare what's left. You can also compare $A-B$ to $0$: positive means A, negative means B.
tips.example: A: $3^{11}$, B: $4\times3^{10}$. Divide both by $3^{10}$: A becomes $3$, B becomes $4$, so **B**. Same idea: A: $\frac{n}{n+1}$, B: $\frac{n+1}{n+2}$ for a positive $n$. $B-A=\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}>0$, so **B**.

tips.title: Square both sides to clear roots
tips.text: **When:** both quantities are sums of square roots and **both are positive**. **Do:** square each one. The bigger square belongs to the bigger number. Use $(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2$: often the plain parts match and only the middle term decides.
tips.example: A: $\sqrt5+\sqrt7$, B: $\sqrt3+3$. A$^2=12+2\sqrt{35}$, B$^2=3+9+2\sqrt{27}=12+2\sqrt{27}$. $\sqrt{35}>\sqrt{27}$, so **A**. Don't square if a side could be negative: $-3<2$ but $9>4$.

tips.title: Fractions: benchmark, then cross-multiply
tips.text: **When:** you compare two fractions. **Do:** first compare each to an easy number like $\frac12$ or $1$. If they land on different sides, you're done. If not, cross-multiply (the bottoms must be positive). **Shortcut:** adding the same positive number to the top and bottom pulls a fraction **toward 1**, so $\frac79<\frac{8}{10}$ but $\frac97>\frac{10}{8}$.
tips.example: A: $\frac{13}{27}$, B: $\frac{15}{29}$. Half of 27 is $13.5$, so A is under $\frac12$; half of 29 is $14.5$, so B is over. **B**. For $\frac{17}{35}$ vs $\frac{19}{40}$ (both under $\frac12$): $17\times40=680$ and $19\times35=665$, so $\frac{17}{35}$ is bigger.

tips.title: Long sums: pair the terms
tips.text: **When:** each quantity is a long sum, like all the evens against all the odds. **Do:** don't add anything up. Line the terms up one-to-one, see how much each pair differs, then multiply by the number of pairs.
tips.example: A: $2+4+\cdots+100$, B: $1+3+\cdots+99$. Pair $2$ with $1$, $4$ with $3$, and so on: 50 pairs, each A term $1$ bigger. A is $50$ more, so **A**.

tips.title: Same total: closer numbers give a bigger product
tips.text: **When:** two numbers have a fixed sum and you compare their product (or the area of rectangles with a fixed perimeter). **Then:** the product is biggest when the numbers are **equal**, and shrinks as they spread apart. Watch for 'different numbers' or 'whole numbers' in the facts, which can stop you from reaching the top.
tips.example: $x+y=10$. Compare A: $xy$, B: $25$. At $x=y=5$, $xy=25$; any other pair gives less ($6\times4=24$). So A can equal B or be smaller: **(D)**. Add '$x\ne y$' and it becomes **B**.

tips.title: Percents of unknown amounts
tips.text: **When:** the question gives percents but not what they're percents **of**. **Then:** a bigger percent doesn't mean a bigger amount. Unless the two starting amounts are linked, the answer is usually (D). Try one case with equal starting amounts and one with very different ones.
tips.example: Ann's pay went up $10\%$ and Ben's $20\%$. Compare A: the size of Ann's raise, B: the size of Ben's. If both earn 100, B wins (10 vs 20). If Ann earns 1,000 and Ben 100, A wins (100 vs 20). **(D)**.

patterns.title: Repeating decimal to fraction
patterns.idea: Call the decimal $x$. Multiply by $10$ once for each repeating digit (so by 10, 100 or 1,000), then subtract $x$. The endless tail cancels, leaving the repeating block over that many 9s.

cases.name: 1 repeating digit
cases.q: Write $0.\overline{7}$ as a fraction.
cases.spot: one digit repeats, so multiply by $10$.
steps: $10x=7.\overline{7}$ and $x=0.\overline{7}$.
$10x-x=9x=7$, so $x=\mathbf{\frac79}$.

cases.name: 2 repeating digits
cases.q: Write $0.\overline{36}$ as a fraction.
cases.spot: two digits repeat, so multiply by $100$.
steps: $100x=36.\overline{36}$ and $x=0.\overline{36}$.

cases.name: 3 repeating digits
cases.q: Write $0.\overline{123}$ as a fraction.
cases.spot: three digits repeat, so multiply by $1{,}000$.
steps: $1000x=123.\overline{123}$ and $x=0.\overline{123}$.

notWhen: Digits before the repeat starts, like $0.1\overline{6}$: shift the decimal past them first ($10x=1.\overline{6}$), then use the 9s rule ($x=\frac{1}{10}\cdot\frac{15}{9}=\frac16$).
